This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Northwestern University (STU00219535) and written, informed consent was provided by all subjects before any study procedures took place.
Twenty-seven individuals with relapsing-remitting or secondary-progressive multiple sclerosis were recruited for this study.
Participants completed two five-day arms, separated by a washout period of at least four weeks.

Scanning occurred at a different site to the intervention sessions and motor function assessments, and participants were transported between the two sites in a wheelchair with the support of a clinical aide.
Overall study design is shown in Panel A; following an initial screening visit, participants completed two study arms in a randomized order, separated by at least four weeks.

Grey shading indicates when participants were breathing air from an altitude generator; the generator was calibrated to output hypoxic (9% O 2 ) air for AIH therapy sessions and normoxic (21% O 2 ) for sham therapy sessions.
Participants were seated and fit with a non-rebreathing face mask through which gas mixtures were delivered.
Participants were given the chance to practice this task outside of the scanner before each session to ensure comfort and understanding.
Four subjects discontinued study participation due to scheduling conflicts.
Twenty-three subjects completed both treatment arms, and their data were included in analyses.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<0.05", Text = "Minimum cluster size was determined from estimated spatial autocorrelation and generated ANOVA results were thresholded and clustered at α<0.05 (bi-sided, NN=1); p<0.001 was used for activation maps and p<0.05 was used for changes in activation (3dFWHMx, 3dClustSim, 3dClusterize, AFNI)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) therapy is a promising neurorehabilitative intervention with welldocumented improvement in motor function in people with spinal cord injury.

Its effect on lower-limb motor control in multiple sclerosis (MS), where walking impairment is a leading source of disability, remain uncharacterized, and the supraspinal effects of AIH therapy are unknown.

In a sham-controlled, double-blind crossover trial (NCT05164705), 23 adults with MS completed 5 sessions of AIH therapy and of sham therapy; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed before and after each therapeutic intervention.
At each timepoint, blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) functional MRI was collected during a repeated plantar-and dorsi-flexion task.
Task-evoked activation was modeled at the group level and compared across timepoint and therapeutic arm.
Activation changes differed for the leftand right-foot task.
AIH augmented activation in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cortical motor regions during left-foot movement with similar but sub-threshold patterns for the right foot.

Right-foot movement additionally showed enhanced deactivation in prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortices, although these effects were primarily in white matter voxels, limiting their interpretability.

These findings suggest that changes in subcortical activation may contribute to motor function improvements following AIH therapy, implicating the basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical motor loop as a target of AIH-induced neuroplasticity.
These results also indicate that AIH therapy modulates supraspinal motor circuitry, supporting further investigation of the cortical and subcortical effects of this emerging therapeutic treatment.
Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) is an emerging rehabilitative therapy that drives neuroplastic changes and supports motor recovery in the damaged central nervous system 1 .
text.formatted: Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) is an emerging rehabilitative therapy that drives neuroplastic changes and supports motor recovery in the damaged central nervous system <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: It consists of brief, repeated exposures to low oxygen (~9% O 2 ) alternating with periods of normoxia.

The hypoxic stimulus activates chemoreflex-driven serotonergic neurons in the raphe nuclei, triggering synthesis of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and enhancing motoneuron excitability 2, 3 .
text.formatted: The hypoxic stimulus activates chemoreflex-driven serotonergic neurons in the raphe nuclei, triggering synthesis of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and enhancing motoneuron excitability <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: AIH therapy has been shown to improve walking speed and endurance, joint strength, and dexterity in persons with spinal cord injury, and there is growing interest in expanding the clinical applications of this promising therapeutic intervention 2, [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9] [10] .
text.formatted: AIH therapy has been shown to improve walking speed and endurance, joint strength, and dexterity in persons with spinal cord injury, and there is growing interest in expanding the clinical applications of this promising therapeutic intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> .

text.text: Investigations are needed to determine whether similar mechanisms may promote functional recovery in further populations with impaired motor pathways, including persons with multiple sclerosis (PwMS).
Multiple sclerosis significantly impairs motor function as demyelination and neuroaxonal inflammation disrupt communication between the central nervous system and the musculature 11 .
text.formatted: Multiple sclerosis significantly impairs motor function as demyelination and neuroaxonal inflammation disrupt communication between the central nervous system and the musculature <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Persons with multiple sclerosis experience muscle weakness, pain, spasticity, abnormal reflexes, and poor fine motor control, contributing to difficulty maintaining balance and gait and executing everyday tasks 11, 12 .
text.formatted: Persons with multiple sclerosis experience muscle weakness, pain, spasticity, abnormal reflexes, and poor fine motor control, contributing to difficulty maintaining balance and gait and executing everyday tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Approximately 75% of PwMS have difficulty walking due to sensorimotor impairments 11, 12 .
text.formatted: Approximately 75% of PwMS have difficulty walking due to sensorimotor impairments <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Current treatment strategies for multiple sclerosis focus primarily on suppressing inflammation to mitigate disability progression and strategies to manage symptoms.

Rehabilitation approaches, including physical and occupational therapies and adaptive devices, have been used for decades to help maintain mobility and quality of life, yet these treatment strategies do not target the neuroplastic mechanisms underlying lasting motor function recovery [13] [14] [15] .
text.formatted: Rehabilitation approaches, including physical and occupational therapies and adaptive devices, have been used for decades to help maintain mobility and quality of life, yet these treatment strategies do not target the neuroplastic mechanisms underlying lasting motor function recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> .

text.text: Given that AIH appears to modulate neural transmission in corticospinal circuits involved in motor control, this therapy presents a promising and distinct method of promoting motor function recovery in PwMS, complementary to existing treatments 16, 17.
text.formatted: Given that AIH appears to modulate neural transmission in corticospinal circuits involved in motor control, this therapy presents a promising and distinct method of promoting motor function recovery in PwMS, complementary to existing treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref>.

text.text: Our group has recently presented preliminary evidence that a single session of AIH therapy improves motor function in PwMS, showing increased ankle strength, walking ability, and cognitive processing 18 .
text.formatted: Our group has recently presented preliminary evidence that a single session of AIH therapy improves motor function in PwMS, showing increased ankle strength, walking ability, and cognitive processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: However, relatively little is known about how AIH alters the underlying neural control of movement in these individuals 18, 19 .
text.formatted: However, relatively little is known about how AIH alters the underlying neural control of movement in these individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: While lesions and neurodegeneration may impact the integrity of the corticospinal tract in multiple sclerosis, the disease typically involves more diffuse pathology across the brain and spinal cord 20 .
text.formatted: While lesions and neurodegeneration may impact the integrity of the corticospinal tract in multiple sclerosis, the disease typically involves more diffuse pathology across the brain and spinal cord <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: Thus, while the mechanisms underlying AIH efficacy may overlap between SCI and MS cohorts, this therapy may act through distinct supraspinal pathways in PwMS.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides a noninvasive method of studying neural activity, and when combined with a task, can be used to probe changes in sensorimotor activation [21] [22] [23] .
text.formatted: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides a noninvasive method of studying neural activity, and when combined with a task, can be used to probe changes in sensorimotor activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> .

text.text: Previous fMRI studies have shown that patterns of brain activation during voluntary movement are altered in PwMS, with increases in the magnitude and extent of activation compared to healthy subjects, suggesting compensatory activation and functional reorganization of the brain [24] [25] [26] .

text.text: Understanding how AIH therapy alters neural activation associated with motor tasks in PwMS could provide insight into the mechanisms through which this promising treatment improves motor function, facilitating its translation into clinical rehabilitative practice.
We therefore investigated whether repeated sessions of AIH changed neural activation associated with a lower-limb motor task in PwMS.
We conducted a randomized sham-controlled crossover trial, performing motor-task fMRI at the beginning and end of five sessions of daily AIH (or sham AIH) therapy.
We hypothesized that compensatory neural activation associated with the lower limb motor task would be reduced following AIH therapy.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Northwestern University (STU00219535) and written, informed consent was provided by all subjects before any study procedures took place.
Study activities were performed at the Shirley Ryan AbilityLab and Northwestern University.
Twenty-seven individuals with relapsing-remitting or secondary-progressive multiple sclerosis were recruited for this study.

To be included in the study, participants must have an expanded disability status scale (EDSS) score between 3 and 6.5 and a motor functional system scale (FSS) score between 2 and 4, be between the ages of 18 and 75, free of relapses for at least the past year, safe to be scanned with MRI, and if prescribed dalfampridine, taking the same daily dose for at least two months prior to enrollment.
Individuals with active MS lesions, chronic uncontrolled hypertension or sleep apnea, a history of epilepsy or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or who were pregnant were ineligible.
A randomized, double-blinded, sham-controlled crossover study design was employed.
Participants completed two five-day arms, separated by a washout period of at least four weeks.
The order of interventions was randomized.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging and motor function assessments were performed on Day 1 and Day 5 of each intervention week, and AIH or sham AIH was delivered on Days 1-5 (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: Functional magnetic resonance imaging and motor function assessments were performed on Day 1 and Day 5 of each intervention week, and AIH or sham AIH was delivered on Days 1-5 (Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>).

Each study arm consisted of five days of daily acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) or sham therapy.
Before AIH or sham therapy on Day 1 and after therapy on Day 5 of each arm, MRI scanning was performed and functional outcome measures were collected.
The target respiratory protocols for AIH and sham therapy are shown in Panel B, representing the oxygen content of the air inhaled across time.

Grey shading indicates when participants were breathing air from an altitude generator; the generator was calibrated to output hypoxic (9% O 2 ) air for AIH therapy sessions and normoxic (21% O 2 ) for sham therapy sessions.
Participants underwent 5 sessions each of AIH and sham AIH, with interventions delivered in the morning on consecutive days within each arm.
Participants were seated and fit with a non-rebreathing face mask through which gas mixtures were delivered.

The intermittent hypoxia protocol (Figure 1B) lasted approximately 30 minutes and consisted of 15 bouts of hypoxia (9-10% FiO 2 ) or sham hypoxia (21% FiO 2 ) alternated with bouts of normoxic room air (21% FiO 2 ).

text.text: Hypoxic bout durations were determined individually in each session to achieve a target arterial oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) of 84-88%.

Hypoxic and sham hypoxic air were generated by a hypoxia generator (Hyp-123, Hypoxico Inc), and an oxygen monitor continuously monitored the fraction of inspired oxygen of generated gas mixtures.

Oxyhemoglobin saturation and heart rate were continuously monitored (Masimo Rad-57, Danaher; Nonin 4 in Model 7500 pulse oximeter, Nonin Medical Inc.) and blood pressure was taken before and after each session (Welch-Allyn Connex, Hillrom).
fMRI was performed on Day 1 and Day 5 of each intervention arm.
Scanning was performed on a Siemens 3T Prisma scanner using a 64-channel head coil.

Visual instructions prompted participants to perform fourteen 16-second blocks of unilateral dorsi-and plantar-flexion, paced at 0.5 Hz, with 10-18 seconds of rest between blocks, and alternating sides for each consecutive block.

For the left foot, significant increases in BOLD activation were seen bilaterally in the supplemental motor area, the opercular cortex, the insula, and the pallidum and putamen.

Significant increases were also seen in the ipsilateral caudate and contralateral thalamus, although sub-threshold increases were also seen in the contralateral and ipsilateral sides, respectively, of these regions and in the contralateral primary motor cortex.

Significant decreases were seen with right-foot movement in the bilateral prefrontal and posterior parietal cortices and in the ipsilateral superior and middle temporal gyri, all resulting from enhanced negative activation.
This study examined the effects of AIH therapy on neural activation associated with lower limb motor control in PwMS.

Contrary to our initial hypothesis, significant decreases in gray matter activation in motor regions were not observed following AIH therapy under this experimental design, suggesting that this AIH therapy did not measurably reverse the compensatory cortical activation patterns that have been identified in PwMS during motor task performance.
Instead, the primary effect of AIH therapy in this trial was an increase in activation in the thalamus and basal ganglia regions (putamen, caudate, and pallidum).
These changes may reflect a distinct mechanism by which AIH therapy influences lower limb motor function in MS.
Motor task fMRI in PwMS probes how the brain maintains motor function despite demyelination and axonal loss.
In this study, we examined activation associated with lower-limb movement in PwMS.

Lower-limb tasks are less common than upper-limb and hand tasks due to enhanced task-correlated motion artifacts and difficulty isolating movement to the joint of interest, and few previous studies have examined the neural activation patterns associated with lower-limb motor tasks in PwMS [44] [45] [46] [47] .

text.text: Evidence from upper-limb and hand studies suggest that compensatory activation enables patients to maintain relatively normal motor function, and the few studies that have been performed indicate that compensatory activation patterns are also present for lower-limb movement 24, [38] [39] [40] [44] [45] [46] [47].

text.text: While no control group was included in the present study, comparisons of the BOLD activation evoked by the lower-limb task in this population with previous research and with expected activation patterns suggests that compensatory activation may be present.

Activation was seen in the typical regions activated by this task in healthy controls, i.e. the medial primary and supplemental motor cortices and the primary somatosensory cortex [38] [39] [40] [41] .

text.text: Additional activation was identified bilaterally in the insular, frontal opercular, and parietal opercular (secondary somatosensory) cortices, regions that are commonly implicated in compensatory activation patterns in PwMS [38] [39] [40] [41] .

text.text: The recruitment of additional cortical regions to aid in adequate task performance is unsurprising, given the level of disability in this study cohort and participants' reports of difficulty performing the task.
Neural activation showed both significant increases and significant decreases in the AIH intervention arm versus the sham AIH arm (Figure 5).

BOLD increases were seen bilaterally, with slightly more activation on the side contralateral to the task.
Although increases were seen for both feet, significant clusters of increased activation were only found for the left-foot task.

Given that the majority of the study cohort showed greater motor and sensory deficits on the left side (Table 1, 12 participants with left-sided weakness, 9 with right-sided weakness), there may be greater potential for improvement on this side.

text.text: Increases in activation after AIH therapy compared to sham were detected primarily in the deep grey matter structures of the thalamus, putamen, caudate, and pallidum (Figure 5B).

text.text: These regions comprise key structures of the basal ganglia motor circuit, which coordinates motor control and is particularly involved in the learning, execution, and automation of complex motor functions such as this rhythmic flexion task [48] [49] [50] .

text.text: AIH therapy induces neuroplastic changes by activating serotonergic raphe nuclei, triggering serotonin release and activating serotonin receptors in the neurons to which they project 1, 51, 52 .
text.formatted: AIH therapy induces neuroplastic changes by activating serotonergic raphe nuclei, triggering serotonin release and activating serotonin receptors in the neurons to which they project <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> .

text.text: Many of these serotonergic projections target the basal ganglia, particularly the caudate and putamen 53 .
text.formatted: Many of these serotonergic projections target the basal ganglia, particularly the caudate and putamen <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> .

text.text: Increased activation in these regions by the raphe nuclei may explain the observed increases in BOLD signal following AIH therapy, and these enhancements in activation may reflect additional supraspinal mechanisms through which AIH therapy ultimately achieves improvements in motor function.
Decreases were seen in the posterior parietal lobe, the posterior temporal lobe, and the frontal lobe.

Frontal lobe hyperactivity has been previously associated with task performance in PwMS, and decreases in activation have been found with previous therapeutic techniques, suggesting increased task network efficiency 54 .
text.formatted: Frontal lobe hyperactivity has been previously associated with task performance in PwMS, and decreases in activation have been found with previous therapeutic techniques, suggesting increased task network efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> .

text.text: However, the posterior parietal and occipital lobe activation changes were primarily confined to white matter, with all clusters exceeding 50% white matter overlap.
While white-matter fMRI is increasingly of interest, BOLD signals in white matter are less understood than those in gray matter 55 .
text.formatted: While white-matter fMRI is increasingly of interest, BOLD signals in white matter are less understood than those in gray matter <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: Lower blood flow and weaker hemodynamic responses decrease sensitivity, and the relationship between neural activity and BOLD changes in white matter is not well characterized 55, 56 .
text.formatted: Lower blood flow and weaker hemodynamic responses decrease sensitivity, and the relationship between neural activity and BOLD changes in white matter is not well characterized <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56</ref> .

text.text: Furthermore, BOLD signals in white matter will be influenced by the presence of MS lesions, which alter local energy consumption and uncouple metabolic demand from vascular supply 55, 57 .
text.formatted: Furthermore, BOLD signals in white matter will be influenced by the presence of MS lesions, which alter local energy consumption and uncouple metabolic demand from vascular supply <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57</ref> .

text.text: Negative BOLD signals in white matter have also been associated with changes to blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) compartment volume, rather than neurovascular coupling mechanisms, particularly in voxels with deep medullary veins or located proximal to the boundary between tissue and CSF, where MS lesions are also frequently located 58 .
text.formatted: Negative BOLD signals in white matter have also been associated with changes to blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) compartment volume, rather than neurovascular coupling mechanisms, particularly in voxels with deep medullary veins or located proximal to the boundary between tissue and CSF, where MS lesions are also frequently located <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58</ref> .

text.text: Thus, while they should not be discounted as purely noise, the observed white matter fMRI changes should therefore be interpreted with caution, particularly at the lower field strength and spatial resolution used in this study.
Future studies specifically investigating white-matter fMRI changes in MS could clarify interpretation.
Cerebrovascular changes may also contribute to changes in activation seen with AIH therapy.

MS has been associated with cerebrovascular abnormalities, including hypoperfusion and reduced cerebrovascular reactivity, and MS lesions typically form around a central vein, demonstrating that there is a significant vascular component to the disease [59] [60] [61] .
text.formatted: MS has been associated with cerebrovascular abnormalities, including hypoperfusion and reduced cerebrovascular reactivity, and MS lesions typically form around a central vein, demonstrating that there is a significant vascular component to the disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref> .

text.text: While changes to whole-brain cerebrovascular function have not previously been seen with AIH therapy in healthy adults, supporting the safety profile of this intervention, we have shown that 12 sessions of AIH enhance focal perfusion to bilateral sensorimotor cortices 62 .
text.formatted: While changes to whole-brain cerebrovascular function have not previously been seen with AIH therapy in healthy adults, supporting the safety profile of this intervention, we have shown that 12 sessions of AIH enhance focal perfusion to bilateral sensorimotor cortices <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62</ref> .

text.text: The specific cerebrovascular impact of AIH in MS, as well as an understanding of how these changes may influence fMRI activation mapping, will be important targets in future research.
While fatigue was not measured under the present experimental design, it is likely that our experimental protocol modulated fatigue.
The post-intervention scans were performed at the end of a long study visit, after both the AIH therapy and extended functional motor outcome assessments.

Anecdotally, participants reported a) feeling tired at the end of the day and b) feeling less tired following what they believed was the true AIH intervention arm (note, the sham AIH is widely accepted to be indistinguishable from the true AIH intervention in practice).

Thus, the unintentional fatiguing effects of our experimental design may drive some of the brain changes observed in the sham intervention arm (e.g., reduced deactivation of the precuneus for both left and right foot motor tasks).

Furthermore, a major effect of the true AIH intervention may be to simply mitigate those effects, as the precuneus was not significantly different between pre-and post-intervention scans in the AIH arm.

The precuneus is part of the DMN, which has previously been implicated in fatigue in PwMS, with individuals experiencing greater fatigue displaying lower functional connectivity of the DMN and basal ganglia [63] [64] [65] .
text.formatted: The precuneus is part of the DMN, which has previously been implicated in fatigue in PwMS, with individuals experiencing greater fatigue displaying lower functional connectivity of the DMN and basal ganglia <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[63]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[64]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[65]</ref> .

text.text: However, the observed changes in taskevoked negative signal changes in this study cannot be directly compared to such literature reports of resting state functional connectivity.
Neural activation in the basal ganglia has also been inversely related to the severity of fatigue in neurological disorders 66, 67 .
text.formatted: Neural activation in the basal ganglia has also been inversely related to the severity of fatigue in neurological disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">66,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">67</ref> .

text.text: Reductions in basal ganglia connectivity and lower activation of the basal ganglia during cognitive tasks have been associated with greater subjective and objective measures of fatigue in multiple sclerosis, suggesting that dysfunction in these regions may be foundational to central fatigue in MS 68, 69 .
text.formatted: Reductions in basal ganglia connectivity and lower activation of the basal ganglia during cognitive tasks have been associated with greater subjective and objective measures of fatigue in multiple sclerosis, suggesting that dysfunction in these regions may be foundational to central fatigue in MS <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">68,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">69</ref> .

text.text: We observed that AIH increased activation of the thalamus, putamen, pallidum, and caudate significantly more than the sham intervention, again suggesting that this intervention may have a beneficial effect on mitigating fatigue.

However, measures of fatigue were not obtained in this study, Future work should obtain measures of cognitive and physical fatigue to explore whether this intervention is a viable therapy to modulate central fatigue in MS and other neurological disorders.
Limitations of this experimental design present further opportunities for future studies of the effect of therapeutic AIH on motor control in PwMS.

This preliminary crossover trial did not include measurements of task performance during the MRI; it is possible that participants' performance of the ankle flexion task improved with AIH therapy and with practice, and changes in task activation may reflect this improvement.

Anecdotal reports from participants suggested that they felt they could perform the task better, and future studies should include quantitative measures of this task performance for incorporation in fMRI analysis to account for this.
This study did not include a concurrent training component.
Therapeutic AIH has been found to have a synergistic effect with motor training, priming the motor system to enhance the outcomes that can be obtained from solely AIH therapy or motor training 17 .
text.formatted: Therapeutic AIH has been found to have a synergistic effect with motor training, priming the motor system to enhance the outcomes that can be obtained from solely AIH therapy or motor training <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: Although we did observe increased ankle flexion strength in this study following AIH therapy alone (functional outcomes will be reported separately), future trials combining AIH with training will be necessary to evaluate whether the neural changes we have observed relate to meaningful functional improvement (e.g., walking and balance).
The fMRI acquisition was limited in spatial coverage and in spatial resolution.
The acquisition did not include the cerebellum in most participants, and it was therefore excluded from analyses.
The cerebellum is highly involved in motor control, with particular importance in coordination, balance, and motor learning 70 .
text.formatted: The cerebellum is highly involved in motor control, with particular importance in coordination, balance, and motor learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">70</ref> .

text.text: Cerebellar pathology is common in MS, causing gait and coordination problems, tremor, and ataxia as well as cognitive problems due to lesions, atrophy, and disruptions to cerebellar connectivity 71- 73 .
text.formatted: Cerebellar pathology is common in MS, causing gait and coordination problems, tremor, and ataxia as well as cognitive problems due to lesions, atrophy, and disruptions to cerebellar connectivity <ref type="bibr">71- 73</ref> .

text.text: The cerebellum is directly linked to the raphe nuclei, which act as the central command center modulating neuroplasticity, but no study to date has assessed cerebellar changes with AIH therapy 2, 74 .
text.formatted: The cerebellum is directly linked to the raphe nuclei, which act as the central command center modulating neuroplasticity, but no study to date has assessed cerebellar changes with AIH therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">74</ref> .

text.text: Future work should investigate the effects of AIH therapy in the cerebellum.
The voxel spatial resolution implemented in this study also did not allow for detailed investigation of the small subcortical regions that showed the greatest changes with the intervention.

Future studies of the supraspinal effects of AIH therapy with MRI should implement a smaller voxel size to allow for more accurate localization and coregistration of these salient structures, increasing confidence in analyses of subcortical activation changes.
Finally, MS lesion load, lesion location, and the subsequent motor impairments are highly variable across individuals.

Precision mapping in fMRI is becoming increasingly practical with technological and analytical advancements, and single-subject activation in subcortical structures can be robustly detected with approximately 30 minutes of multi-echo fMRI data 75 .
text.formatted: Precision mapping in fMRI is becoming increasingly practical with technological and analytical advancements, and single-subject activation in subcortical structures can be robustly detected with approximately 30 minutes of multi-echo fMRI data <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">75</ref> .

text.text: Precision mapping approaches would eliminate need to average across the inter-subject variability introduced by MS pathology and could further help to clarify known variability in the efficacy of AIH treatment, as previous studies have reported substantial inter-individual variability in treatment response magnitude 2, 76 .
text.formatted: Precision mapping approaches would eliminate need to average across the inter-subject variability introduced by MS pathology and could further help to clarify known variability in the efficacy of AIH treatment, as previous studies have reported substantial inter-individual variability in treatment response magnitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">76</ref> .

text.text: Future work should consider applying precision mapping fMRI techniques to studies of supraspinal changes in neural control of movement with AIH therapy.
Further study of the neuroplastic changes associated with AIH therapy in MS is needed to clarify how the alterations observed here relate to behavioral and functional outcomes.

This preliminary crossover trial suggests that neuroimaging may play a valuable role both in identifying candidates likely to respond to AIH therapy and in optimizing AIH protocol parameters to enhance efficacy, positioning basal ganglia activation as a potential candidate biomarker for future trials combining AIH with structured motor rehabilitation.
